answer.rationale: The single most load-bearing inherited claim is memory_c2, because it is the only thing that makes switching the primary vendor look safe, and it is exactly the claim I would be over-extending: it records a cost win and clean invoicing, but says nothing about whether that vendor sustained volume at 94% line utilization with zero buffer, nor whether the switched category was delivery-critical. So I pull its original record. Second I pull memory_c4, because renegotiation is the action I actually intend and I want to know whether the recovered margin came from a genuine benchmarked concession or from scope/quality being quietly narrowed, which memory_c4's summary would not show. Given one decision this cycle: switching primary supply 14 days before expiry, into a line with no buffer, converts a pure cost problem into a delivery-risk problem, which the stated objective forbids; the mandate says cut 18% of spend, not cut it by migration. Negotiating with the incumbent, using the low-cost quote as a live benchmark (memory_c4) and volume-term leverage (memory_c6), can capture most of the mandate while memory_c1's stable integration is retained. I keep it a guarded, short-term commitment rather than a multi-year lock so the switch option and memory_c3's second-source play stay available at the next review. Uncertainty preserved: I do not treat the low-cost vendor as proven at committed volume, and if negotiation lands short of 18% I will report the shortfall rather than absorb it by accepting a risky switch or an unverified scope reduction.
